To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) there is no high-pressure metamorphism in the High Himalaya, (b) there is no metamorphic overprint on the High Himalayan gneisses in the Everest–Kathmandu area, (c) there is a large amount of ductile thrusting in eastern Nepal, and (d) the MCT postdates the metamorphism in the gneisses.

The major observed thrusting on the Main Central thrust (MCT) in eastern Nepal post-dates the Barrovian type metamorphism of the high Himalaya gneiss, and this result, at variance to the famous reverse metamorphism model, better explains the abnormal superposition of metamorphic events in the Himalayas.

the main Himalayan orogenic belt is a stack of tectonic slabs, each with its own metamorphic history, and that the metamorphic evolution of these slabs was strongly affected by the tectonic processes of Himalayan orogeny.

the tectonic and microstructural study of a major ductile thrust shear zone in the eastern Nepal Himalayas.

the MCT postdates the Barrowian metamorphic event in the Himalaya, and that the MCT thrusting has been responsible for the observed pressure and temperature variations in the High Himalaya.

(1) there is no evidence that the Himalayas are a "reverse" metamorphic terrain; (2) there is evidence of late metamorphic thrust faulting in eastern Nepal; and (3) the Himalayan gneisses are an allochtonous slab, and not a root of a metamorphic pile.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the main thrusting of the High Himalayan slab occurred after the Barrovian-type metamorphism.
the Himalayan thrusts are not only of the "classic" kind but that they are also of the ductile type, which explains the large amount of shortening and the abnormal metamorphic overprint.
the Himalayas are a thrust stack, the thrusts of which were active at different times.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Himalayas are a very complicated region with many different tectonic and metamorphic processes going on at the same time.
the MCT shear-zone is a ductile shear zone, and not a simple thrust fault, which is the usual way it is depicted on geological cross sections of the Himalaya.

the Himalayan metamorphic core complex is a tectonometamorphic unit that has experienced a complex evolution in which a large part of its deformation and metamorphism occurred after the main Himalayan collision.
